title: What is the Strategy pattern, where does it appear in the Java standard library, and how does it enforce the Open/Closed Principle (payment-strategy example)?
shortTitle: What is the Strategy pattern and how does it enforce the Open/Closed Principle

s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The Strategy pattern defines a family of interchangeable algorithms behind a common interface and lets the algorithm be selected at runtime. The client holds a reference to the strategy interface and delegates to whichever concrete strategy it was given, without knowing which one. It appears throughout the Java standard library, most clearly as Comparator, and it enforces the Open/Closed Principle because adding a new algorithm means adding a new strategy class rather than editing existing code.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** When Rajesh pays at the National Bank of India, he can choose UPI, card, or net banking. The payment counter does not care which he picks; it just runs whatever payment method he hands it. Each payment method is a self-contained strategy, and adding a new one, like a wallet, means opening a new method lane without touching the existing lanes. The counter stays the same; only the chosen method changes.

**One line to remember:** Strategy makes algorithms interchangeable behind one interface, chosen at runtime, so adding a new algorithm is a new class, never an edit to old code.

sections.s2_technical:
Strategy has three parts: a strategy interface that declares the algorithm, concrete strategies that implement it differently, and a context that holds a strategy and delegates to it. For example `interface PaymentStrategy { void pay(BigDecimal amount); }` with concrete UpiPayment, CardPayment, and NetBankingPayment, and a PaymentContext that calls `strategy.pay(amount)`.

The key behavior is that the algorithm is selected at runtime and the context is decoupled from the concrete algorithm. The context depends only on the interface, so you can swap strategies without changing the context: `context.setStrategy(new UpiPayment()); context.checkout(amount)` and later `context.setStrategy(new CardPayment())`.

In the Java standard library, Strategy is everywhere. Comparator is the clearest example: `list.sort(Comparator.comparing(Account::getBalance))` plugs a comparison algorithm into a fixed sort. The ThreadPoolExecutor takes a RejectedExecutionHandler, which is a strategy for what to do when the queue is full. Layout managers in Swing, and the various Collectors in the streams API, are strategies. Even Runnable passed to a thread is a pluggable unit of behavior.

Strategy enforces the Open/Closed Principle directly. Open for extension means I can add a new payment method; closed for modification means I do not touch the tested code to do it. Without Strategy, a payment method would be a growing switch: `if (type == UPI) ... else if (type == CARD) ...`, and every new method edits that switch, risking the existing branches. With Strategy, a new WalletPayment is a new class that implements PaymentStrategy, registered in a map or injected as a bean, and the context and existing strategies are never touched.

A concrete payment example shows the win. The checkout service holds a `PaymentStrategy`, chosen from the customer's selection. Adding wallet support is literally adding WalletPayment and registering it; the checkout code is unchanged, so there is nothing to re-test in the existing flow and no chance of breaking UPI or card.

A senior nuance: in modern Java a Strategy is frequently just a lambda or a method reference, because a single-method interface is a functional interface. So `PaymentStrategy upi = amount -> gateway.chargeUpi(amount)` is a strategy without a named class. In Spring, injecting a `Map<String, PaymentStrategy>` gives runtime selection by bean name for free, which is the cleanest production form and makes the Open/Closed benefit automatic.
sections.s3_banking:
The National Bank of India's checkout service lets customers pay bills and transfers using different payment methods.

Problem 1 — The payment code was a growing switch. Originally the checkout had a big if-else on payment type. Every time the bank added a method, a developer edited that switch, and once a careless edit broke the card branch while adding net banking, causing failed card payments in production. This is the exact pain that Strategy with Open/Closed removes.

Problem 2 — Choosing the method at runtime. Rajesh picks UPI while Priya picks card, and the choice is known only at request time from the customer's selection. The checkout needs to run the chosen algorithm without knowing which one. This is what the Strategy context does.

Problem 3 — Adding a wallet without risk. The bank wants to add a wallet payment next sprint without re-testing or risking UPI and card. With Strategy, that is a new class and a registration, with zero edits to existing payment code, which is the Open/Closed guarantee.

The demo defines a PaymentStrategy interface, concrete UPI, card, and net banking strategies, a checkout context that selects by a map, processes payments for Rajesh and Priya, and then adds a wallet strategy to prove that extension requires no edits to existing code.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash

mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: three payments with different methods, a wallet method added at runtime, and a list of amounts to sort.

Step 1: The CheckoutService is created and registers the three built-in strategies in a map keyed by method name: UPI, CARD, and NETBANKING. The context now holds all known algorithms behind the PaymentStrategy interface.

Step 2: checkout is called with method UPI for Rajesh. The context looks up UPI in the map, finds the UpiPayment strategy, and delegates by calling pay. The context never names UpiPayment; it only knows the interface. The UPI charge is logged.

Step 3: checkout is called with CARD for Priya. The exact same context code runs, but this time the map returns CardPayment, which applies a card charge with a fee note. The behavior differed entirely by which strategy was selected, with no branching in the context.

Step 4: checkout is called with NETBANKING for Rajesh. Again the same code path selects the NetBankingPayment strategy and runs it. Three different algorithms ran through one unchanged method.

Step 5: A WALLET strategy is registered at runtime as a lambda. This is the Open/Closed moment: a brand-new payment method was added without editing the context, the interface, or any existing strategy. The registry simply gained one entry.

Step 6: checkout runs with WALLET, the map returns the lambda strategy, and the wallet charge is logged. The new method works immediately, and nothing in the tested UPI or card path was touched, so there is nothing to re-test there.

Step 7: Finally a list of amounts is sorted with Comparator.naturalOrder, which is the JDK's Strategy: a comparison algorithm plugged into a fixed sort. The sorted list is logged, showing Strategy appearing in the standard library, not just in our code.

Final output:

```
2026-10-26 09:10:45 [INFO] Account SAV2001 paying via UPI
2026-10-26 09:10:45 [INFO] UPI charge Rs.50000
2026-10-26 09:10:45 [INFO] Account CUR3001 paying via CARD

2026-10-26 09:10:45 [INFO] Account SAV2001 paying via NETBANKING

2026-10-26 09:10:45 [INFO] Account SAV2001 paying via WALLET

```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: checkout(method, account, amount)
    │
    ▼
  CheckoutService (context)
    │ registry.get(method) → PaymentStrategy (interface)
    ▼
  strategy.pay(amount)   ← context delegates, no concrete knowledge
    │
    ├─ "UPI"        → UpiPayment.pay()
    ├─ "CARD"       → CardPayment.pay()
    ├─ "NETBANKING" → NetBankingPayment.pay()
    └─ "WALLET"     → lambda strategy (added at runtime)
    │
    ▼
  OPEN/CLOSED: register("WALLET", lambda) → no edit to context/old strategies
  JDK Strategy: amounts.sort(Comparator.naturalOrder())
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The Strategy pattern defines a family of interchangeable algorithms behind a common interface and lets me choose the algorithm at runtime. It has three parts: a strategy interface that declares the algorithm, concrete strategies that implement it differently, and a context that holds a strategy and delegates to it without knowing which concrete one it has. The whole point is that the context depends only on the interface, so I can swap algorithms freely.

It appears all over the Java standard library. The clearest example is Comparator, where I plug a comparison algorithm into a fixed sort with something like sort by balance. The thread pool's RejectedExecutionHandler is a strategy for what to do when the queue is full, the Collectors in the streams API are strategies, and even a Runnable handed to a thread is a pluggable unit of behavior. Recognizing these shows I understand Strategy as something the language itself relies on, not just a textbook diagram.

Strategy enforces the Open/Closed Principle directly, and the payment example makes it concrete. Open for extension means I can add a new payment method; closed for modification means I do not touch the tested code to do it. Without Strategy, the payment method is a growing switch on type, and every new method edits that switch and risks breaking the existing branches. In fact at the National Bank of India we once broke the card branch while adding net banking to such a switch, which caused failed card payments in production. With Strategy, each method is its own class implementing PaymentStrategy, the checkout context just looks it up and delegates, and adding a wallet method is a new class registered in a map, with zero edits to the context or the existing strategies, so there is nothing in the old flow to re-test.

The senior point I add is that in modern Java a Strategy is often just a lambda, because a single-method interface is a functional interface, so I can write a payment strategy as a one-line lambda. And in Spring I usually get runtime selection for free by injecting a Map of method name to PaymentStrategy bean, so adding a payment method is literally adding a new bean. That is the cleanest production form, and it makes the Open/Closed benefit automatic, which is exactly why Strategy is one of the patterns I reach for most often.

---

keyPoints: S: Single Responsibility — one class, one reason to change
O: Open/Closed — open for extension, closed for modification
L: Liskov Substitution — subtypes must be substitutable for base types
I: Interface Segregation — many specific interfaces over one general
D: Dependency Inversion — depend on abstractions, not concrete classes
